title: The Sentence
summary: A sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense. Sentences are grouped by what they do.
points: Assertive (declarative): makes a statement and ends with a full stop.
Interrogative: asks a question and ends with a question mark.
Imperative: gives a command, request or advice.
Exclamatory: shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.
examples: She is singing. (assertive)
Is she singing? (interrogative)
Sing now. (imperative)
How well she sings! (exclamatory)
tip: Look at the purpose of the sentence, not only its punctuation.

title: Subject and Predicate
summary: Every sentence has two parts: the subject, which is what the sentence is about, and the predicate, which tells us what is said about the subject.
points: The simple subject is the main noun or pronoun. The complete subject includes its describing words.
The simple predicate is the main verb. The complete predicate includes the verb and everything that goes with it.
Find the verb first, then ask who or what does it, to find the subject.
examples: The old man walked slowly home. Subject: The old man. Predicate: walked slowly home. Simple subject: man. Simple predicate: walked.
tip: Ask Who or what? before the verb to find the subject.

title: Phrase and Clause
summary: A phrase is a group of words without its own subject and finite verb. A clause has a subject and a finite verb.
points: A phrase works as one part of speech: a noun phrase, an adjective phrase or an adverb phrase.
A main (principal) clause makes sense on its own.
A subordinate clause depends on the main clause and works as a noun, adjective or adverb.
examples: In the morning (phrase, adverb). I know that he is honest. (main clause plus subordinate noun clause)
tip: If the group has a finite verb with its own subject, it is a clause. If not, it is a phrase.

title: Parts of Speech
summary: English has eight parts of speech. Each word's part of speech depends on the job it does in its sentence.
points: Noun: names a person, place, thing or idea.
Pronoun: replaces a noun.
Adjective: describes a noun or pronoun.
Verb: shows action or state.
Adverb: describes a verb, adjective or another adverb.
Preposition: shows the relation between a noun or pronoun and another word.
Conjunction: joins words, phrases or clauses.
Interjection: shows sudden feeling.
examples: The boy (noun) ran (verb) quickly (adverb).
tip: The same word can change its part of speech. Check how it is used in the sentence.

title: The Noun: Kinds of Nouns
summary: Nouns are grouped into five kinds.
points: Proper noun: the name of one particular person, place or thing (Delhi, Ganga). It starts with a capital letter.
Common noun: a general name (city, river).
Collective noun: a group seen as one (army, flock, class).
Material noun: a substance (gold, milk, wood).
Abstract noun: a quality, state or action (honesty, joy, sleep).
examples: Delhi is a city. Gold is precious. Honesty is the best policy.
tip: You can count a common noun (two cats), but not usually a material or abstract noun.

title: The Noun: Gender
summary: Gender tells us whether a noun refers to a male, a female, either, or no living being.
points: Masculine: male beings (boy, king).
Feminine: female beings (girl, queen).
Common: either sex (parent, teacher, cousin).
Neuter: things without sex (book, table).
examples: Feminine forms can be made in three ways: different words (king, queen), a suffix (actor, actress; lion, lioness), or a prefix (he-goat, she-goat).
tip: Learn the common pairs: king/queen, boy/girl, nephew/niece, horse/mare.

title: The Noun: Number
summary: Number tells us whether a noun means one (singular) or more than one (plural).
points: Most nouns add -s (cat, cats).
Nouns ending in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch or -x add -es (bus, buses; box, boxes).
A consonant followed by y changes to -ies (city, cities).
Some nouns change completely (child, children; man, men; mouse, mice).
Some nouns are the same in both numbers (sheep, deer).
examples: One leaf, two leaves. One knife, many knives.
tip: Some nouns are always plural, such as scissors and trousers.

title: The Noun: Case
summary: Case shows how a noun or pronoun is used in a sentence.
points: Nominative case: the doer of the action, or the subject.
Objective case: the receiver of the action, or the object of a verb or preposition.
Possessive case: shows ownership, with an apostrophe and s (Ram's bat) or with of (the bat of Ram).
Some grammars also name a vocative case, used when calling someone (Ram, come here).
examples: Ram (nominative) kicked the ball (objective).
This is Ram's bat (possessive).
tip: Ask who receives the action. That noun is in the objective case.

title: The Adjective
summary: An adjective describes a noun or pronoun. It tells what kind, how many, or which one.
points: Adjective of quality: a red rose, a kind man.
Adjective of quantity: some water, much money.
Adjective of number: three boys, many books.
Demonstrative adjective: this book, those boys.
Possessive adjective: my pen, their house.
examples: She wore a red dress. Three students passed.
tip: An adjective answers which one, what kind, or how many about a noun.

title: Comparison of Adjectives
summary: Adjectives change form to compare things. There are three degrees: positive, comparative and superlative.
points: Positive: describes one thing (tall).
Comparative: compares two things, with -er or more (taller, more beautiful).
Superlative: compares three or more, with -est or most (tallest, most beautiful).
Some adjectives are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; little, less, least.
examples: Ram is taller than Shyam. Ram is the tallest of the three boys.
tip: Use the comparative with two things, and the superlative with three or more.

title: Adjectives Used as Nouns
summary: Some adjectives can stand for a group of people or a quality, with the word the before them.
points: The rich, the poor, the wise: these mean groups of people.
They take a plural verb when they mean a group.
Some stand for a quality, such as the true or the beautiful.
examples: The poor are often neglected.
The wise listen before they speak.
tip: If you can add men, people or ones after the adjective, it is probably used as a noun.

title: Position of Adjectives
summary: Adjectives usually come before the noun. In some cases they come after it.
points: Before the noun: a clever boy.
After a linking verb: the boy is clever.
After the noun in fixed phrases: something new, God Almighty, heir apparent, court martial.
After enough: a man brave enough.
examples: The sky looked dark. She is strong enough to lift it.
tip: Most adjectives in English go before the noun. Learn the fixed phrases as set expressions.

title: Correct Use of Some Adjectives
summary: Some adjectives must be followed by a particular preposition, and some pairs are often confused.
points: Use the right preposition after an adjective: different from, averse to, capable of, worthy of, fond of.
Use fewer with things you can count and less with amounts: fewer mistakes, less water.
Use each other for two people and one another for more than two.
examples: His answer is different from mine. She is fond of music.
tip: When in doubt, check the adjective's usual preposition in a dictionary.

title: Articles
summary: The words a, an and the are articles. A and an are the indefinite article, and the is the definite article.
points: Use a before a consonant sound (a boy, a university) and an before a vowel sound (an apple, an hour).
Use the for a specific or known thing (the sun, the book I bought).
Use no article for general plural or uncountable ideas (Boys like games. Gold is precious).
examples: He is an honest man. The honest man is respected.
tip: The article depends on the sound of the next word, not its spelling.

title: Personal Pronouns
summary: Personal pronouns stand for the speaker, the person spoken to, or the person or thing spoken about.
points: First person: I, we. Second person: you. Third person: he, she, it, they.
A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces (its antecedent) in person, number and gender.
Each pronoun changes form with its case: I, me, my; he, him, his; we, us, our.
examples: Ram lost his pen. The girls lost their bags.
tip: After it is or it was, formal writing uses the subject form: It is I.

title: Reflexive and Emphatic Pronouns
summary: Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves and point back to the subject. Emphatic pronouns add force to a noun.
points: Reflexive: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object are the same person: She hurt herself.
Emphatic: the same words used to stress a noun: I myself saw it.
examples: He cut himself. The Principal himself came.
tip: Do not use hisself or theirselves. They are not correct.

title: Demonstrative, Indefinite and Distributive Pronouns
summary: These three groups of pronouns point out, refer loosely, or refer to each member of a group.
points: Demonstrative: this, that, these, those, which point to things.
Indefinite: one, some, any, none, somebody, everyone, which do not name a specific person or thing.
Distributive: each, every, either, neither, which refer to members of a group one by one.
examples: This is my book. Each of the boys has a bat. Neither of them came.
tip: Each, every, either and neither are singular, so use a singular verb with them.

title: Relative Pronouns
summary: A relative pronoun joins a relative clause to the noun it describes.
points: Who: for people. Which: for things and animals. That: for people or things.
Whose: shows possession. Whom: the object form for people.
Use that after words like all, only, very and superlatives.
examples: The boy who came first won. The book that I read was good.
The man whose car was stolen called the police.
tip: The relative pronoun comes right after the noun it describes.

title: Interrogative Pronouns
summary: Interrogative pronouns ask questions: who, whom, whose, which and what.
points: Who is the subject of a question (Who is there?).
Whom is the object (Whom did you call?).
Whose asks about ownership (Whose pen is this?).
Which and what ask for a choice from a group (Which do you want?).
examples: What is your name? Whom did you meet?
tip: If the answer would be he, she or they, use who. If it would be him, her or them, use whom.

title: Transitive and Intransitive Verbs
summary: A transitive verb needs an object to complete its meaning. An intransitive verb does not.
points: Transitive: she reads a book. The verb reads needs the object a book.
Intransitive: the baby sleeps. No object is needed.
Some verbs are both, depending on the sentence: He runs fast (intransitive). He runs a shop (transitive).
examples: The dog barked. The dog chased the cat.
tip: Ask what or whom after the verb. If you get an answer, the verb is transitive.

title: Verbs of Incomplete Predication
summary: Some verbs do not make full sense on their own. They need a complement to complete the meaning.
points: Linking verbs such as be, become, seem, appear, remain, look, feel and grow need a complement: He became a doctor.
Verbs such as call, make and elect take an object and then a complement: They elected him captain.
examples: She seems happy. The people made him their leader.
tip: The complement describes or renames the subject or object. It is not an object.

title: Active and Passive Voice
summary: In the active voice the subject does the action. In the passive voice the subject receives the action.
points: The passive is formed with a form of be and the past participle: is written, was written, has been written.
The object of the active becomes the subject of the passive.
The doer comes after by in the passive, or is left out.
examples: Ram wrote the letter. (active)
The letter was written by Ram. (passive)
tip: Keep the same tense when you change the voice. Only the verb form changes.

title: Mood
summary: Mood shows the attitude of the speaker: a fact, a command, or a wish or doubt.
points: Indicative: states a fact or asks a question (He is here.).
Imperative: gives a command or request (Come here.).
Subjunctive: expresses a wish or a condition that is not true (If I were you, I would go.).
examples: If he were rich, he would help. (subjunctive)
tip: In the subjunctive, use were for all persons after if in a condition that is not true.

title: Tenses: Introduction
summary: Tense shows when an action happens. There are three main times, and each has four forms.
points: Main times: present, past and future.
Forms: simple, continuous (progressive), perfect and perfect continuous.
Example with write: I write; I am writing; I have written; I have been writing.
examples: She sings. She is singing. She has sung. She has been singing.
tip: Learn the three main times first, then add the four forms to each.

title: The Uses of the Present and Past Tenses
summary: Each present and past tense has its own use. Choosing the right one makes the meaning clear.
points: Simple present: habits and general truths (The sun rises in the east.).
Present continuous: an action happening now (She is reading.).
Simple past: a finished action at a stated time (I saw him yesterday.).
Past continuous: an action in progress at a past time (I was reading when you called.).
examples: I have lived here since 2010. (present perfect, since a point in time)
tip: Do not use the simple past with a time that continues to now, like since or for. Use the present perfect.

title: The Future
summary: English has several ways to speak about the future. The most common are shall, will and going to.
points: Simple future: I and we use shall; other persons use will.
For determination, promise or command, the words are reversed: I will do it; you shall pass.
Going to is used for plans and intentions (I am going to visit my aunt).
The present continuous shows arranged future events (We are leaving tomorrow).
examples: I shall go tomorrow. He will come soon.
tip: For a plan you have already made, going to or the present continuous is natural.

title: The Verb: Person and Number
summary: A verb must agree with its subject in person and number.
points: A singular subject takes a singular verb: he goes, the boy is.
A plural subject takes a plural verb: they go, the boys are.
Two singular subjects joined by and take a plural verb. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
A collective noun takes a singular verb when the group acts as one.
examples: Neither the teacher nor the students are ready.
The jury is divided.
tip: Find the true subject first. Words between the subject and verb do not change the agreement.

title: The Infinitive
summary: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, usually with to: to go, to eat.
points: As a noun: To err is human.
As an adjective: a book to read.
As an adverb of purpose: He works to earn money.
Bare infinitive (without to) comes after modal verbs and after make, let, see and hear.
examples: I want to sleep. You must help her. I saw him cross the road.
tip: After modal verbs like can, must and will, use the bare infinitive, without to.

title: The Participle
summary: A participle is a verb form that works as an adjective. There are three kinds.
points: Present participle: ends in -ing and shows action in progress (the running water).
Past participle: usually ends in -ed, or is an irregular form, and shows a completed action (the broken window).
Perfect participle: having plus the past participle, showing an action finished before the main verb (Having finished the work, she went home).
examples: Seen from the hill, the town looked small.
tip: A participle describes a noun or pronoun. A gerund, which also ends in -ing, is used as a noun.

title: The Gerund
summary: A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used as a noun.
points: As subject: Swimming is good exercise.
As object of a verb: She enjoys reading.
As object of a preposition: He is fond of singing.
Do not confuse it with a participle, which describes a noun.
examples: Walking is healthy. (gerund, subject) The walking man is my uncle. (participle, describes man)
tip: If you can replace the word with a thing, like exercise, it is a gerund.

title: Irregular Verbs
summary: Irregular verbs do not add -ed for the past tense and past participle. Their forms must be learned.
points: Learn the three forms: base, past, past participle.
Examples: go, went, gone; write, wrote, written; begin, began, begun.
Other examples: eat, ate, eaten; drink, drank, drunk; see, saw, seen.
examples: I have gone there. He wrote a letter yesterday.
tip: Never use the past form after have or has. Use the past participle: have written, not have wrote.

title: Auxiliaries and Modals
summary: Auxiliary verbs help the main verb. Modal verbs add meaning such as ability, permission or obligation.
points: Auxiliaries: be, have, do.
Modals: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to.
Modals do not add -s for he or she, and they are followed by the bare infinitive.
examples: She can swim. You must finish your work. He does not know.
tip: After a modal, use the base verb without to: You should go, not should to go.

title: Conjugation of the Verb Love
summary: Conjugation shows the forms of a verb across tenses and persons. The verb love is used as the model.
points: Present: I love, you love, he loves, we love, they love.
Past: I loved, he loved.
Future: I shall love, he will love.
Perfect: I have loved, he has loved.
examples: I have loved this song since childhood.
tip: Practise one tense at a time, reading all the persons aloud.

title: The Adverb
summary: An adverb tells more about a verb, an adjective or another adverb. It answers how, when, where, how often or how much.
points: Manner: quickly, well. Place: here, outside. Time: now, yesterday. Frequency: often, always.
Degree: very, quite, too. It can modify an adjective or another adverb.
Some adverbs modify the whole sentence: Perhaps he is right.
examples: He runs very fast. She came yesterday.
tip: If the word describes a verb, it is probably an adverb, even if it looks like an adjective.

title: Comparison of Adverbs
summary: Adverbs compare in the same three degrees as adjectives, but many use more and most.
points: Short adverbs take -er and -est: fast, faster, fastest.
Most -ly adverbs use more and most: carefully, more carefully, most carefully.
Irregular: well, better, best; badly, worse, worst; little, less, least.
examples: He ran faster than his brother. She sings most beautifully.
tip: Do not use both -er and more together. Choose one.

title: Formation of Adverbs
summary: Many adverbs are made by adding -ly to an adjective. Some spelling changes are needed.
points: Most adjectives add -ly: quick, quickly; slow, slowly.
Adjectives ending in -y change to -ily: happy, happily.
Adjectives ending in -le drop the e and add -y: gentle, gently.
Some adverbs look the same as their adjectives: fast, early, hard, late. Hardly means almost not, and is a different word.
examples: He works hard. She is hardly ever late.
tip: Hardly does not mean hard. Hardly means almost not.

title: Position of Adverbs
summary: Where an adverb goes in a sentence changes the emphasis. There are common patterns.
points: Adverbs of frequency usually go before the main verb but after the auxiliary: He often goes. He has often gone.
Adverbs of manner usually go after the object: He sang the song well.
Adverbs of degree go before the adjective or adverb they modify: very good, quite fast.
examples: She always takes the bus. They walked slowly home.
tip: Put the adverb close to the word it describes, so the meaning is clear.

title: The Preposition
summary: A preposition shows the relation between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence.
points: Common prepositions: in, on, at, by, for, with, from, to, of, under, over.
Simple: in, at. Compound: into, within. Phrase: in front of, because of.
The noun or pronoun after a preposition is its object, and it takes the objective form: between you and me.
examples: The book is on the table. She sat between him and me.
tip: Use the objective form after a preposition: with him, not with he.

title: Words Followed by Prepositions
summary: Many verbs and adjectives always go with one particular preposition. These pairs must be learned.
points: Verb + preposition: depend on, rely on, consist of, believe in, apologise to, prefer X to Y.
Adjective + preposition: good at, afraid of, fond of, interested in, responsible for, capable of.
The same verb can take different prepositions with different meanings: look at, look for, look after.
examples: He is good at mathematics. She is afraid of dogs.
tip: Learn each pair as one phrase, not as two separate words.

title: The Conjunction
summary: A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses.
points: Co-ordinating conjunctions join equal parts: and, but, or, nor, for, yet, so, and the pairs either...or, neither...nor, both...and.
Subordinating conjunctions join a subordinate clause to the main clause: that, if, though, because, when, while, since, till, unless, before, after.
Use the right conjunction for the meaning: but shows contrast, so shows result, because shows cause.
examples: I was tired, so I slept early. (co-ordinating) I slept early because I was tired. (subordinating)
tip: If the two parts could stand alone as sentences and are equal, a co-ordinating conjunction joins them.

title: Some Conjunctions and Their Uses
summary: Some conjunctions have more than one use. Their meaning in the sentence decides which one is right.
points: Since can show time (since Monday) or reason (since you are tired).
Lest means so that not, and is followed by should or a verb: He fled lest he should be caught.
Till and until have the same meaning and both are correct.
Than and as join two parts of a comparison: He is taller than I am.
examples: I have not seen him since he left. Since you are here, let us begin.
tip: Read the sentence again with the meaning in mind before you choose.

title: The Interjection
summary: An interjection is a word or short phrase that shows sudden feeling. It does not join the rest of the sentence.
points: Common interjections: Oh!, Alas!, Hurrah!, Bravo!, Hush!, Ah!
Use an exclamation mark after strong feeling, and a comma after a mild one.
An interjection stands alone and is not linked to the grammar of the sentence.
examples: Alas! He is gone. Hurrah! We won the match.
tip: If the word shows a feeling and stands alone, it is an interjection.

title: The Same Word Used as Different Parts of Speech
summary: One word can be a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition or conjunction. Its job in the sentence decides its part of speech.
points: Before: preposition (before the wedding), adverb (I have seen it before), conjunction (before I leave).
Since: preposition (since Monday), adverb (I have not seen him since), conjunction (since you are here).
Light: noun (the light), adjective (a light bag), verb (to light a lamp).
Run: verb (to run), noun (a run in the park).
examples: He came after me. (preposition, followed by a pronoun)
He came after the rain had stopped. (conjunction, followed by a clause)
He came later. (adverb, no object or clause)
tip: Ask what the word is joined to. A noun after it means preposition; a clause after it means conjunction.
